text: In a new ad for the sports betting platform Novik, actress Sydney Sweeney wears little to no clothing while posing with sports gear. It's racked up 35 million views on Instagram in just four days. Now athletes are hitting back online by posting their own takes on what it looks like to be a woman in sports. Australian surfer Felicity Palmatier is one of them. Just absolute utter disbelief, incredibly disappointing, like how far you can put women's sports backwards in the space of a 40-second commercial. So Sydney Sweeney recently appeared in an advertisement for Novik, a sports protection and betting platform. In the ad, she poses with different pieces of sporting equipment while wearing little to no clothing. And it created an enormous backlash, particularly from female athletes and influencers. They argue that the ad sexualizes women in sports and reduces women to their bodies instead of celebrating their talent, dedication, and athletic achievements. And look, I understand that concern. Women in sports have historically struggled to receive attention for their athletic ability rather than simply their appearance. But if you are trying to criticize Sydney for supposedly setting women's sports backwards, you have to be consistent. Otherwise, this starts to look incredibly hypocritical. And the irony begins with the athlete you just saw. Felicity Palmatier previously created a four-minute film called Skin Dip, in which she serves completely naked, not simply in a bikini, completely naked. She described it as an artistic exploration of her relationship with the ocean and said that the process was incredibly empowering. Now, she says Sydney appearing naked alongside sporting equipment is incredibly disappointing and puts women's sports backwards. And Palmatier is hardly the only example. ESPN published its body issue for more than a decade, featuring prominent female athletes completely naked. Serena Williams, Ronda Rousey, Megan Rapinoe, Sue Bird, Hope Solo, Candice Parker, Miesha Tate, and many others participated. Now, supporters will say that was different. The purpose was to celebrate the incredible power of the athletic body and explain the athlete's personal journeys. And fine, there is some truth in that distinction. But let's be honest about what the overwhelming majority of ordinary viewers saw. They saw famous athletes posing naked in a commercial sports publication. The artistic explanation didn't make them any less naked. But even if we completely disregard ESPN, how do we explain all the female athletes who appeared in publications specifically designed to be sexually provocative? Two-time Olympic figure skating champion Katerina Witt, seven-time Olympic swimming medalist Amanda Beard, and quite a few other professional athletes, including tennis player Ashley Hackelrode, boxer Mia St. John, and volleyball player Gabriela Riz, have all posed nude for Playboy. Sports Illustrated photographed athletes including Ronda Rousey, Lindsay Vaughn, Karolina Wozniacki, and Alex Morgan wearing nothing except painted-on swimsuits. Maria Sharapova, Serena Williams, Venus Williams, and Danica Patrick also appeared in a swimsuit issue. For years, women exposing their bodies on camera has frequently been defended as confidence, bodily autonomy, and female empowerment. But when Sidney Sweeney makes the same choice, it supposedly becomes a devastating setback for women? Again, you are allowed to dislike the ad. You can criticize appearing naked next to sporting equipment. But then apply that principle consistently. Something tells me that at least part of this outrage is not simply about what was done, but about who did it. Sidney Sweeney is white, conventionally attractive, registered as a Republican, and has increasingly been associated with a political right. Would the reaction have been exactly the same if a proudly progressive actress had made this advertisement? What if it had featured a woman of color or a plus-size actress and had been presented as confidence and body positivity? In the heart of hearts, what do you think? My point is not that every sexualized advertisement is empowering or that every criticism of one is wrong. My point is much simpler. You cannot celebrate women displaying their bodies as empowerment when you approve of the woman and then call it degrading when you do not. Have whatever standard you want, just apply it consistently.
